lessons.title: Prepositions that always take Akkusativ
lessons.summary: Seven little words that push the next noun into the Akkusativ automatically — the meaning is irrelevant, you just learn the list.
lessons.rule:
A preposition is one of those small words that sits in front of a noun and states the relation: for you, without sugar, through the city. Turkish does this job with an ending glued onto the word (şekersiz) or with a word that follows it (senin için). German puts it in front, like English — but charges you one extra fee.

In German every preposition owns a case. A case is just the small change German makes to the article in front of a noun depending on the noun's job: der Mann can become den Mann or dem Mann. Normally you have to work the case out from the meaning. After a preposition you work out nothing — the preposition has already decided, and you obey.

Seven prepositions always demand the Akkusativ. Not usually. Not when something moves. Always. Learn them as one block: FUDGEBO — für, um, durch, gegen, entlang, bis, ohne.

Luckily the Akkusativ is the cheap case, because only the masculine visibly changes: der → den, ein → einen, mein → meinen. Feminine, neuter and plural look exactly like the dictionary form. Pronouns do change, though, and this is where people get caught: ich → mich, du → dich, er → ihn, wir → uns. You say für dich, never für du.

Two footnotes. entlang is the odd one out: it stands after its noun — die Straße entlang, not entlang die Straße. And bis usually appears bare in front of a time or a place — bis morgen, bis Berlin. If a second preposition follows, that second one takes over: bis zum Bahnhof is Dativ, because zu is in charge now.

tables.title: FUDGEBO — the seven
rows: um die Ecke, um acht Uhr
gegen die Wand, gegen acht Uhr

examples.note: für always takes the Akkusativ, so du has to turn into dich.
der Bruder is masculine, and masculine is the one thing the Akkusativ visibly changes: mein → meinen.
die Stadt is feminine, so it looks untouched — but it is still Akkusativ, not Nominativ.

examples.de: Der Supermarkt ist um die Ecke.
examples.en: The supermarket is around the corner.
examples.note: Nothing moves at all here, and it is still Akkusativ. The preposition decides, not the meaning.
gegen forces the Akkusativ, and er becomes ihn.
entlang comes after its noun, and die Straße is Akkusativ all the same.

mistakes.why: Pronouns take the case too, not just articles. After für, du must become dich.
der Bruder is masculine, and masculine after an Akkusativ preposition adds -en: mein → meinen.
durch is fixed Akkusativ. It does not matter that you are walking around inside a place — the list wins, always.
entlang is the one preposition on this list that stands behind its noun, exactly like a Turkish postposition.

drills.question: Das Geschenk ist für ___.
drills.explain: für is on the Akkusativ list, and the Akkusativ form of du is dich.

drills.question: Wir gehen durch ___ Park.
drills.explain: durch always takes the Akkusativ, and masculine is the only form that visibly changes: der → den.

drills.question: Ich fahre ohne ___ Auto. (mein)
drills.explain: das Auto is neuter, and neuter looks identical in the Akkusativ, so there is no ending to add.

drills.question: Der Bäcker ist um ___ Ecke.
drills.explain: Nothing is moving, but um demands the Akkusativ anyway; feminine simply looks the same as the Nominativ.

drills.question: Ich habe nichts gegen ___. (er)
drills.explain: gegen takes the Akkusativ, and er is the pronoun that changes most obviously: er → ihn.

drills.question: Ich kaufe ein Buch für ___ Vater.
drills.explain: der Vater is masculine and für is an Akkusativ preposition, so mein takes the -en ending.

drills.answer: Ich habe ein Geschenk für dich
drills.explain: The verb stays in second position, the thing you have follows, and the für-phrase closes the sentence.
entlang is the only one of the seven that stands behind its noun, and die Straße is still Akkusativ.

lessons.title: Prepositions that always take Dativ
lessons.summary: The chant every German schoolchild knows — aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu — plus the contractions you cannot avoid and the nach/zu/in trap.
lessons.rule:
Same deal as the last lesson, different case. These prepositions do not think either: whatever noun follows them goes into the Dativ, every single time, whatever the sentence means.

The core list is chanted in German schools as seven words in a row: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu. Say it out loud until it sounds like one long word. Then add three quieter ones you will still meet weekly: gegenüber (opposite), ab (from … onwards), außer (except).

The Dativ changes more than the Akkusativ did, so there is more to see: der → dem, die → der, das → dem, and plural die → den with an extra -n on the noun itself, as in mit den Kindern. Pronouns: ich → mir, du → dir, er → ihm, sie → ihr, wir → uns.

Four of these fuse with the article in everyday speech, and the fused form is not optional — the long version sounds like you are pointing at one specific thing:

  • zu dem → zum — zum Arzt
  • zu der → zur — zur Arbeit
  • von dem → vom — vom Bahnhof
  • bei dem → beim — beim Chef

Now the part that trips up everybody living in Germany: how to say to a place. German splits it three ways. Use nach for towns and countries that have no article — nach Berlin, nach Deutschland — plus the fixed phrase nach Hause. Use zu for people, shops and institutions you are heading for — zum Arzt, zur Arbeit, zu Anna. Use in when you actually go inside something, and for countries that carry an article — in die Stadt, in den Supermarkt, in die Türkei. Watch out: that last in is not on this list and takes the Akkusativ instead. The next lesson is entirely about it.

tables.title: The ten Dativ prepositions
rows: out of / from (where you come from)

tables.title: Going to a place: nach, zu or in?
rows: towns and countries with no article, plus nach Hause
people, shops, doctors, work — a destination as a point
when you go inside, and countries with an article

examples.de: Ich fahre mit dem Bus zur Arbeit.
examples.en: I go to work by bus.
examples.note: mit is automatic Dativ (der Bus → dem Bus), and zu der Arbeit has to shrink to zur.
aus takes the Dativ, and the feminine Dativ is der — the same word as the masculine Nominativ.

examples.en: I'm going to the doctor tomorrow.
examples.note: zu + dem = zum. Nobody says zu dem Arzt in normal speech.

examples.de: Ich wohne seit einem Jahr in Berlin.
examples.en: I've been living in Berlin for a year.
examples.note: seit is Dativ, so ein Jahr becomes einem Jahr — and German uses the present tense here, not the past.
In the Dativ plural the noun itself picks up an extra -n, not just the article.

examples.de: Nach der Arbeit fahre ich nach Hause.
examples.note: The same word twice: nach der Arbeit means 'after', nach Hause is a fixed phrase for 'home' with no article at all.

mistakes.why: den is the Akkusativ. mit is always Dativ, and masculine Dativ is dem.
Cities and countries without an article take nach. Keep zu for people and buildings: zum Arzt, zu Anna.
zu and dem must contract in ordinary speech. The long form sounds like you mean that one particular supermarket over there.
The Dativ plural marks twice: -n on the article word and -n on the noun.

drills.question: Ich fahre mit ___ Bus.
drills.explain: mit is always Dativ, and masculine Dativ is dem — den would be the Akkusativ.

drills.question: Sie kommt aus ___ Türkei.
drills.explain: aus takes the Dativ, and the feminine Dativ is der even though it looks like a masculine article.

drills.question: Ich gehe morgen ___ Arzt. (zu + dem)
drills.explain: zu and dem fuse into zum in normal German; the long form would sound like one specific doctor.

drills.question: Wir fahren im Sommer ___ Italien.
drills.explain: Countries and cities that carry no article take nach, never zu or in.

drills.question: Ich wohne seit ___ Jahr in Hamburg.
drills.explain: seit is a Dativ preposition, and das Jahr is neuter, so ein becomes einem.

drills.question: Ich gehe jetzt ___ Arbeit.
drills.explain: die Arbeit is feminine, so zu + der contracts to zur.

drills.answer: Ich fahre mit dem Zug nach Hamburg
drills.explain: The verb sits in position two, then how you travel, then where you are going — manner before place.

drills.answer: Nach der Arbeit gehe ich nach Hause
drills.explain: When a time phrase opens the sentence the verb must still be the second element, so the subject slides in behind it.

lessons.title: The two-way prepositions — in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen
lessons.summary: Nine prepositions that take either case, and the single question — wohin? or wo? — that decides which one.
lessons.rule:
Nine prepositions refuse to pick a side. They take the Akkusativ sometimes and the Dativ other times, and the very same words mean two different things depending on which one you choose. They are: in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen.

There is exactly one test and it takes two seconds. Ask the sentence a question:

  • wohin? — where to? Something ends up in a new place. → Akkusativ: Ich gehe in die Küche.
  • wo? — where? You are only reporting a position. → Dativ: Ich bin in der Küche.

Read the next bit slowly, because it is the trap that catches everyone: the test is not "is anything moving". It is "does something cross into a new place". Ich schwimme im See is full of movement, but all of it happens inside the lake and I never enter the lake during the sentence — Dativ. Ich springe in den See — now I cross the edge and end up somewhere I was not before — Akkusativ.

The verb usually gives the answer away. sein, bleiben, wohnen, arbeiten, stehen, liegen, sitzen, warten describe a position → Dativ. gehen, fahren, kommen, stellen, legen, setzen, hängen put something somewhere new → Akkusativ. German even keeps two versions of the same idea: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch (it is lying there) against Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch (I am putting it there).

Several of these fuse with the article, and the short form hands you the case for free: ins and ans are Akkusativ, im and am are Dativ. So Ich gehe ins Kino means you are on your way to the cinema, and Ich bin im Kino means you are already sitting inside it. One letter, a completely different sentence.

tables.title: The nine, both ways
rows: Ich lege es auf den Tisch.
Die Lampe hängt über dem Tisch.
Die Katze läuft unter das Bett.
Die Katze schläft unter dem Bett.
Ich stelle das Auto vor das Haus.
Das Auto steht vor dem Haus.
Der Garten ist hinter dem Haus.
Ich stelle den Stuhl neben das Bett.
Der Stuhl steht neben dem Bett.
Ich stelle den Stuhl zwischen die Betten.
Der Stuhl steht zwischen den Betten.

tables.title: The contractions give the case away

examples.note: wohin? I end up in a room I was not in before, so in takes the Akkusativ: die.
wo? Pure position, nothing changes place, so in takes the Dativ: der.

examples.de: Ich lege das Handy auf den Tisch.
examples.en: I'm putting the phone on the table.
examples.note: The phone travels onto the table, so auf takes the Akkusativ: der Tisch → den Tisch.

examples.de: Das Handy liegt auf dem Tisch.
examples.en: The phone is lying on the table.
examples.note: Same table, same preposition — but this is only a report of where it is, so dem.
Plenty of movement, but all of it inside the lake, so this is still wo? and stays Dativ.

examples.de: Heute Abend gehen wir ins Kino.
examples.en: This evening we're going to the cinema.
examples.note: in + das = ins, and the form ins already tells you the case is Akkusativ.

mistakes.why: gehen takes you somewhere new — wohin? — so the Akkusativ is needed. in der Küche would mean you are wandering around inside it.
sein only states where you are — wo? — so it is Dativ. Learners overuse the Akkusativ because in die Stadt is such a common phrase.
The test is not 'is there movement' but 'do you cross into a new place'. Swimming happens inside the lake, so it is Dativ.
in and das contract to ins in normal speech. The long form sounds like you are pointing at one particular cinema.

drills.question: Ich gehe in ___ Küche.
drills.explain: Ask wohin? — you end up in a new room, so in takes the Akkusativ.

drills.question: Ich bin in ___ Küche.
drills.explain: Ask wo? — sein only reports a position, so in takes the Dativ.

drills.question: Das Buch liegt auf ___ Tisch. (der Tisch)
drills.explain: liegen describes something resting where it already is, so this is wo? and auf takes the Dativ.

drills.question: Heute Abend gehen wir ___ Kino.
drills.explain: You are travelling to the cinema, so it is wohin?, and in + das becomes ins.

drills.question: Ich warte ___ Bahnhof. (an + dem)
drills.explain: Waiting is standing still, so an takes the Dativ dem, and the two contract to am.

drills.question: Die Katze läuft unter ___ Bett.
drills.explain: The cat ends up somewhere new, so this is Akkusativ — neuter just happens to look unchanged.

drills.answer: Ich stelle die Flasche auf den Tisch
drills.explain: stellen puts something in a new place, so auf takes the Akkusativ den.

drills.answer: Das Auto steht vor dem Haus
drills.explain: stehen only reports a position, so vor takes the Dativ dem.
